h1: Complex number to rectangular form Calculator
summary: The Complex number to rectangular form calculator turns the magnitude and the phase into real part (a). It suits a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Complex number to rectangular form calculator work?
sections.html:
The Complex number to rectangular form calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports real part (a) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the magnitude (r) and the phase (φ).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in degrees. The unit chip switches it to any of the 12 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Complex number to rectangular form calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Real part (a)=(magnitude (r) × the cosine of (phase (φ)))
Imaginary part (b)=(magnitude (r) × the sine of (phase (φ)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Magnitude (r) = 10 and Phase (φ) = 10 deg. Working through the relationship above gives Real part (a) = 9.8481 and Imaginary part (b) = 1.7365.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Real part (a) = 9.8481 and Imaginary part (b) = 1.7365 should be roughly the size you expected from Magnitude (r) = 10 and Phase (φ) = 10 deg.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Angle, opening in degrees

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Complex number to rectangular form calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the magnitude and the phase — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Complex number to rectangular form calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — magnitude for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Switch the units to the ones you normally use and confirm the numbers are unchanged apart from their label; if they are not, a chip was on the wrong setting.

faq.q: What does the Complex number to rectangular form calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns real part (a), derived from the magnitude and the phase. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Complex number to rectangular form calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the magnitude and the phase, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter phase (φ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Phase (φ) opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Real part (a) = 9.8481. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Complex number to rectangular form calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
